summary: The writer reviews The Hobbit by J. R. R. Tolkien, a book that brings back childhood memories, and describes it as a prequel to The Lord of the Rings about Bilbo Baggins (whom the text calls a dwarf)

Gandalf persuades Bilbo to join him and the dwarfs on an adventure, taking him from his hobbit hole to battles with creatures and monsters, with the goal of defeating the dragon Smaug and reclaiming the dwarves' gold
The writer considers Bilbo one of the most heroic fictional characters, an ordinary man who is transformed
The book taught the writer values such as humility, respect for kin and courage, and the writer believes it remains relevant for young people
arguments: The book is special because of the euphoria and excitement it gave the writer as a child; its intense moments kept the writer hooked
Bilbo is one of the most heroic fictional characters because he changes from an ordinary man into a benevolent hero
The characters teach valuable lessons: staying humble, respecting your kin and finding the courage to take on any challenge
The book remains relevant for future young readers because of its lessons and the mix of feelings it creates (melancholy, merriness, bafflement, adrenaline)
arguments_main: Names the book's valuable lessons or its lasting relevance for young readers as the most important argument (Bilbo as a hero is also acceptable)
